name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q01 - Logical sequence for writing Lewis dot structures

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the correct logical sequence for writing the Lewis dot structure of a covalent molecule or polyatomic ion:

P. Place the least electronegative atom in the central position and write the skeletal structure.
Q. Utilize remaining electron pairs for multiple bonding or as lone pairs so that each bonded atom attains an octet.
R. Sum the valence electrons of all combining atoms, adjusting for any negative or positive ionic charges.
S. Distribute shared electron pairs to form single bonds between the atoms in the skeletal structure.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Writing a Lewis dot structure requires knowing the total electron budget first, establishing the atomic connectivity, placing single bonds, and finally completing octets with lone pairs or multiple bonds.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequencing
First, count the total number of valence electrons available by adding the valence electrons of the combining atoms and adding electrons for anions or subtracting for cations.
Second, write the skeletal structure by placing the least electronegative atom in the central position and more electronegative atoms at terminal positions.
Third, account for the shared pairs of electrons required to form single covalent bonds between adjacent atoms.
Fourth, distribute the remaining electron pairs either as lone pairs or for multiple bonding so that every bonded atom attains an octet (or duplet for hydrogen).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of steps is: summing valence electrons (adjusting for charge) \(\rightarrow\) writing the skeletal structure with the least electronegative central atom \(\rightarrow\) assigning single-bond electron pairs \(\rightarrow\) completing octets using remaining lone pairs or multiple bonds (R, P, S, Q).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q02 - Decreasing order of electron-pair repulsions in VSEPR theory

questiontext.text: According to VSEPR theory, what is the correct order of decreasing repulsive interaction between electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In VSEPR theory, lone pairs (\(\mathrm{lp}\)) are localised on a single central atom and therefore occupy more angular space than bond pairs (\(\mathrm{bp}\)), which are shared between two nuclei.

Step 2: Evaluation of Repulsions
Because a lone-pair electron cloud is broader and closer to the central nucleus, the repulsion between two lone pairs (\(\mathrm{lp-lp}\)) is the strongest. The repulsion between a lone pair and a bond pair (\(\mathrm{lp-bp}\)) is intermediate, and the repulsion between two bond pairs (\(\mathrm{bp-bp}\)) is the weakest.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order of repulsive interactions is \(\mathrm{lp-lp} > \mathrm{lp-bp} > \mathrm{bp-bp}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing order of carbon-carbon covalent bond lengths

questiontext.text: Arrange the carbon–carbon covalent bonds \(\mathrm{C-C}\), \(\mathrm{C=C}\), and \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\) in the correct order of increasing bond length.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As the bond order (number of shared electron pairs between two atoms) increases, the nuclei are pulled closer together, causing the bond length to decrease.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bond Lengths
- \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\) has bond order \(3\) and an average bond length of \(120\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- \(\mathrm{C=C}\) has bond order \(2\) and an average bond length of \(133\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- \(\mathrm{C-C}\) has bond order \(1\) and an average bond length of \(154\ \mathrm{pm}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Arranging from shortest to longest gives the increasing bond length order: \(\mathrm{C\equiv C} < \mathrm{C=C} < \mathrm{C-C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q04 - Increasing energy order of molecular orbitals in dinitrogen

questiontext.text: For the \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) molecule, what is the correct order of increasing energy of the molecular orbitals \(\sigma^{*} 2s\), \(\pi 2p_{x}\), \(\sigma 2p_{z}\), and \(\pi^{*} 2p_{x}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For homonuclear diatomic molecules up to \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) (namely \(\mathrm{Li}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{Be}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\)), \(2s\text{-}2p\) mixing raises the energy of the \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) molecular orbital above the degenerate \(\pi 2p_{x}\) and \(\pi 2p_{y}\) bonding molecular orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of Orbital Energies
The complete increasing energy sequence for \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) is:
\[\sigma 1s < \sigma^{*} 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^{*} 2s < (\pi 2p_{x} = \pi 2p_{y}) < \sigma 2p_{z} < (\pi^{*} 2p_{x} = \pi^{*} 2p_{y}) < \sigma^{*} 2p_{z}\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Selecting the four specified orbitals in increasing order of energy gives \(\sigma^{*} 2s < \pi 2p_{x} < \sigma 2p_{z} < \pi^{*} 2p_{x}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q05 - Increasing bond angle in methane, ethene, and ethyne

questiontext.text: Arrange the hydrocarbons \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4}\), and \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}\) in the correct order of increasing bond angle around the carbon atom.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As the \(s\)-character in carbon hybrid orbitals increases from \(sp^{3}\) (\(25\%\)) to \(sp^{2}\) (\(33.3\%\)) to \(sp\) (\(50\%\)), the hybrid orbitals move further apart in space and the bond angle increases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Molecule
- In \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\), carbon is \(sp^{3}\) hybridised (tetrahedral), with \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angle \(= 109.5^{\circ}\).
- In \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4}\), each carbon is \(sp^{2}\) hybridised (trigonal planar), with \(\mathrm{H-C-H}\) bond angle \(= 117.6^{\circ}\) (and \(\mathrm{H-C-C} = 121^{\circ}\)).
- In \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}\), each carbon is \(sp\) hybridised (linear), with \(\mathrm{H-C-C}\) bond angle \(= 180^{\circ}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of increasing bond angle around carbon is \(\mathrm{CH}_{4} < \mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4} < \mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q06 - Increasing order of dipole moment in hydrogen halides

questiontext.text: Arrange the hydrogen halides \(\mathrm{HF}\), \(\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{HBr}\), and \(\mathrm{HI}\) in the correct order of increasing dipole moment (\(\mu\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{HX}\)), the dipole moment depends on the product of charge separation and bond length (\(\mu = Q \times r\)). Down the halogen group, electronegativity decreases sharply from \(\mathrm{F}\) to \(\mathrm{I}\), reducing the partial charge \(Q\) and decreasing the net dipole moment.

Step 2: Evaluation of Dipole Moments
The experimental dipole moment values are:
- \(\mathrm{HI}\): \(0.38\ \mathrm{D}\)
- \(\mathrm{HBr}\): \(0.79\ \mathrm{D}\)
- \(\mathrm{HCl}\): \(1.07\ \mathrm{D}\)
- \(\mathrm{HF}\): \(1.78\ \mathrm{D}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct order of increasing dipole moment is \(\mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HF}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q07 - Increasing relative stability of dioxygen and its ions

questiontext.text: Using molecular orbital theory, arrange the species \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\), and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) in the correct order of increasing relative stability.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Relative stability of diatomic species increases with increasing bond order, where \(\mathrm{Bond\ order} = \frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Using the MO configuration of \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\):
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) (\(18\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)): \(N_{b} = 10,\ N_{a} = 8 \Rightarrow \mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 8) = 1.0\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\) (\(17\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)): \(N_{b} = 10,\ N_{a} = 7 \Rightarrow \mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 7) = 1.5\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) (\(16\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)): \(N_{b} = 10,\ N_{a} = 6 \Rightarrow \mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = 2.0\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\) (\(15\ \mathrm{e}^{-}\)): \(N_{b} = 10,\ N_{a} = 5 \Rightarrow \mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 5) = 2.5\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since higher bond order corresponds to greater stability, the increasing order of relative stability is \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-} < \mathrm{O}_{2}^{-} < \mathrm{O}_{2} < \mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q08 - Increasing ionic character of bonds in selected molecules

questiontext.text: Arrange the bonds in the molecules \(\mathrm{LiF}\), \(\mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{O}\), \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{ClF}_{3}\) in the correct order of increasing ionic character.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ionic character of a chemical bond increases with an increase in the electronegativity difference (\(\Delta\chi\)) between the two bonded atoms. Bonds between identical non-metal atoms are purely covalent, while bonds between electropositive alkali metals and highly electronegative non-metals like oxygen or fluorine have the highest ionic character.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Molecule
- \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) contains two identical nitrogen atoms (\(\Delta\chi = 0\)), so it is purely covalent (\(0\%\) ionic character).
- \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\) has polar covalent \(\mathrm{S-O}\) bonds with moderate electronegativity difference.
- \(\mathrm{ClF}_{3}\) involves chlorine bonded to the most electronegative element fluorine, giving slightly higher polar/ionic character than \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\).
- \(\mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) is formed between a strongly electropositive alkali metal (\(\mathrm{K}\)) and strongly electronegative oxygen (\(\mathrm{O}\)), giving high ionic character.
- \(\mathrm{LiF}\) has the highest ionic character among these due to the combination with fluorine, the most electronegative element, yielding the largest electronegativity difference.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of increasing ionic character is \(\mathrm{N}_{2} < \mathrm{SO}_{2} < \mathrm{ClF}_{3} < \mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{O} < \mathrm{LiF}\).
